rationale: B wins because it is cleaner about where the real stories are and more disciplined about proof, especially in "An AI agent now drafts the 'please cancel our contract' email — but a human still has to hit send." A has strong angles, but "Ramp's new AI agent emails vendors to cancel the software nobody's using" steps past the supplied fact that the agent drafts emails for finance approval. The difference is not huge; A is useful, but B has less overclaiming and a sharper business-model lens.
gaps_in_A: "Ramp's new AI agent emails vendors" overstates the fact pattern; the update says it drafts cancellation or renegotiation emails the finance team approves, not that the agent itself sends them.

"As Ramp customers, this beta group presumably already had spend visibility" is doing real work on a presumption. A flags the needed confirmation, but the headline angle depends on an unproven premise.
"An AI agent is now doing part of the procurement analyst's job" is plausible, but it drifts toward labor-substitution without any supplied labor, headcount, or workflow adoption evidence.
The category angle asks for "examples of comparable agentic-AI products elsewhere," which would require outside reporting before the angle is pitch-ready.
gaps_in_B: "the enterprise tier is the real business" is a sharp angle, but it is inference. The update only says an enterprise tier is coming later this year, not that it is the primary monetization strategy.
"long the SaaS vendor's quiet profit center" is good copy, but it is broader industry analysis not proven by the update. It needs a vendor or analyst source before pitching.
"Ramp is giving away the audit and charging for the workflow" implies the enterprise workflow will be charged separately; the facts say a tier is coming, not pricing or packaging.
The next step jumps to `journalist-fit-check` before locking down methodology and a named beta customer; the stronger move is proof first, names second.
